docs.title: One green check for every product
docs.text:
7th Eclipse Tractus-X Community Days · 3–4 December 2026 · ARENA2036, Stuttgart

In about an hour your team builds an end-to-end test for one Eclipse Tractus-X product, with an AI assistant doing the typing and you doing the thinking. You leave with a pull request in that product's repository and a test that runs on every change.

No test framework to learn. No code to write. A laptop and curiosity are enough.

Get started New here? Read the introduction first

docs.title: The problem we solve together
docs.text:
Tractus-X has about thirty products. Each one tests itself. Whether they work together, the way a partner uses them, is checked by people, by hand, in the three weeks before a release.

That is late, and it does not scale. So here is the plan:

Every product keeps an E2E test in its own repository. It is written in one common, tool-independent format, a TCK. It runs in GitHub Actions on every pull request.

Today you write the first one for your product.

docs.title: What you work with
docs.text:
Thing What it is TestLab The open-source test engine of Eclipse Tractus-X. It reads a TCK and runs it. A TCK project A folder of YAML files that describes your test. This is what you commit. The Test Suite IDE A browser tool for building TCK projects with blocks and an AI assistant. One way to get there faster; the files it produces are plain YAML you could also write by hand. A reusable workflow A few lines of GitHub Actions that validate, compile and run your test. The developer toolbox The small Eclipse Tractus-X dataspace the workflow starts in the GitHub runner. What is in it

The IDE in this workshop is provided by the Catena-X Association. The TCK format and TestLab are not tied to one dataspace: the same approach works for tests of other dataspaces and other standards.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the product catalog and look at the first table, Fits the workshop. These products can be built and run with what every team gets.
  2. Give each team one of them. Prefer a product the team maintains or uses.

  3. More teams than products in that table? Choose, in this order:

    Option Cost Give a second team the same product with another scenario from More scenarios None. Two pull requests to one repository: tell its committers. Give a team a product from the second table The team builds and compiles, and skips the run in chapter 6. Deploy more of the Umbrella for the event Your time. See Deploy.

  4. Edit catalog/assignments.json. One entry per team:

    { "team": "team-01", "teamName": "Team 01", "productId": "sldt-digital-twin-registry" }

    team is the short name used for the handout file and the connector inventory. productId is an id from products.json. Add "scenario": "..." when the team takes a scenario other than the product's first one.

  5. Set "sample": false at the top of the file once the real teams are in.

  6. Check the files:

    pip install -r requirements.txt
python catalog/build_catalog.py --check

    It fails with a clear message when a team is listed twice or names a product that does not exist.

  7. Build the handouts.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
What must exist in the Test Suite before the first team sits down.

Home · For administrators

Important

The screens named here were checked on a local Test Suite without connectors, up to the Run button of the dialog. A run to green in a hosted Test Suite is not verified: it is the first item of the dry run. The same test project is verified in GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Per team
docs.text:
Create With Why An organization The team's name Drafts, runs and registered components belong to it A user The account printed in box B One per team is enough; the Driver signs in A plan with the IDE and enough parallel runs For every workshop organization The IDE is not part of every plan, and twenty teams run within ten minutes An app The product's name and a version The run dialog asks for the App under test A connector Name, DSP URL, Participant ID (BPNL) and DID of the team's provider connector The run dialog asks for the EDC Connector A registry, if the team's test uses one Name and Base URL of the team's Digital Twin Registry The run dialog asks for the Digital Twin Registry

A team can register these itself: the run dialog offers Register an app, Register a connector and Register a registry. Doing it for them saves two minutes of the ten in chapter 6.

docs.title: Three things to settle in the dry run
1 · The engine's own connector
docs.text:
The Test Suite's engine runs the tests from its own connector. A team cannot supply that side: values in the infrastructure.engine namespace are refused. So:

  • The engine needs a connector registered for the release the tests declare (saturn). Without it every run fails at once with "requires infrastructure that is not fully bound: engine.connector". This was seen in the dry run.
  • That connector must be a participant of the same dataspace as the teams' connectors: same BDRS, same issuer, credentials issued.

If you give every team a pair, the second connector of each pair is the engine's connector for that team's organization. Box D of the handout then only tells the team who the partner is; nobody types it.

docs.title: 2 · Tests that prepare their own offers
docs.text:
The template and the worked example create an asset, two policies and a contract definition on the team's connector in their setup, and remove them in teardown. That needs the connector's Management API address and key.

The form Register a connector does not ask for them: in a hosted Test Suite the engine normally only negotiates against a connector and never drives it. The engine's interface for registering a connector does accept a management address and a key.

Warning

Not run. Decide in the dry run which of these holds for your deployment:

  • A. Register each team's connector with its management address and key, through the engine's interface. The tests then run unchanged.
  • B. Create the template's asset, policies and contract definition on each team's connector yourself, before the session. The SUT Setup step of the run dialog lists exactly what is expected, with Copy and Download for each definition.
  • C. Skip the run in the IDE, and let every team see its green run in GitHub Actions in chapter 8. This always works.

docs.title: 3 · Addresses must be public host names
docs.text: The engine refuses a run when an input names a host that is not a fully qualified public host name, for example http://my-product:8080. Every address on the handout, including the two "as the connector reaches it", must therefore be a public name such as https://provider-dtr.team-01.example.org/api/v3.

docs.title: The assistant
docs.text:
Nothing is configured for it on the server. Each participant connects a model in the browser, and the key stays there.

Option in the IDE What must be true on your side A GPT or Claude model The venue network lets browsers reach the provider Catena-X AI Participants who use it have their key and agent ID Local / self-hosted LLM The deployed IDE includes the option. A participant's own server must allow the IDE's address as an origin; the IDE's address must be https://.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
What has to run at the venue, in which order, and how to know it works.

Home · For administrators

Important

This page describes what to bring up and how to check it. The connector pair recipe is the one the workflow runs in GitHub Actions, where it is proven. The deployment of the Test Suite itself follows its operators' own runbook, which is not public. Nothing on this page has been run at ARENA2036 yet: do the dry run.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
Piece What it is Who reaches it Test Suite The web application with the IDE, behind a sign-in Participants' browsers Engine The backend that compiles and runs TCKs. It uses TestLab. The Test Suite; it calls the connectors Identity provider Sign-in for the Test Suite, one organization per team Participants' browsers Database Drafts, runs and their traces The engine Connector pairs Per team: two connectors with wallets, a Digital Twin Registry and a BDRS The engine, and each other Hello service One small API for everyone, the target of the first test in chapter 3 Participants' browsers and laptops, and the engine

Placeholders used in this kit: https://ide.example.org for the Test Suite and *.team-01.example.org for a team's connectors. Replace them in your own inventory only, never in this repository.

docs.title: Order
docs.text:
1. Connector pairs first. They take the longest and everything else points at them.
  2. Test Suite, engine, identity provider, database, and the hello service.
  3. Configure: organizations, users, environments. See Configure.
  4. Smoke test from a guest laptop.

docs.title: 1 · Connector pairs
docs.text:
One pair is one small dataspace from the Tractus-X Umbrella, chart version 26.03.00, with its values-adopter-decentralized-identityhub.yaml profile. It gives you:

Role in the tutorial Umbrella name Identity Your side, the system under test provider connector, its wallet and its Digital Twin Registry BPNL000000000001 Partner side, where the test runs from consumer connector and its wallet BPNL000000000002 Shared BDRS, IssuerService

The exact, proven sequence is in the reusable workflow, .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml, from the step "Add Tractus-X Helm repo" to "Preflight — check connector and DTR reachability". Read it as the runbook. Four things the chart does not do for you, and the workflow therefore does itself:

Must be true Why Workflow step The connectors' host names resolve inside the cluster The connectors find each other, their wallets and the issuer by host name "Point in-cluster DNS at the ingress controller" An ingress class is the default Some ingresses of the profile name no class "Install ingress-nginx and make it the default IngressClass" Both participants hold their credentials The chart seeds the claims but does not issue the credentials. Without them every negotiation is refused. "Issue Catena-X credentials to both participants" The connectors' vault secrets exist The data plane signs and verifies its tokens with them "Generate the connectors' in-memory vault secrets"

docs.title: One pair per team
docs.text:
Deploy the release once per team, each in its own namespace and with its own host names.

Warning

Not run. The workflow deploys one pair with fixed host names (provider.local, consumer-dsp.local, …). Several pairs in one cluster need those names changed per team in the Helm values, and the names are also part of the participants' identities. Prove it for two teams before you plan for twenty.

If that does not work in time, the fallback is one shared pair for all teams. It works because each team renames the template's asset and policy ids to its product. Say so on the handouts: every team then has the same boxes C and D.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text: One pair runs on a standard GitHub-hosted runner. There the whole job, from an empty runner to the test result, takes five to six minutes. Plan the cluster from that and from your own measurement of one pair.

docs.title: 2 · The Test Suite
docs.text:
Deploy the Test Suite, its engine, the identity provider and the database with the operators' runbook. For this session it must have:

Requirement Why A public https:// address with a valid certificate Browsers refuse the assistant's calls from an insecure page The IDE switched on for the workshop organizations It is the tool of the session The assistant's Local / self-hosted option included For participants who bring their own model server The engine can reach every team's connectors by the host names on the handout The engine runs the tests Each provider connector can reach the address in box C, "as the connector reaches it" Tests offer the product through the connector's data plane Enough parallel runs for all teams Twenty teams press Run within the same ten minutes

docs.title: The hello service
docs.text:
Chapter 3 starts with a test of a tiny API, before any connector. One instance serves every team. It is a stock unprivileged nginx serving a few JSON files, so it needs no build:

# Set your host name in hello-service/kustomization.yaml first.
kubectl create namespace hello-service
kubectl apply -k e2e-testing/hello-service -n hello-service

Give it a certificate under the secret hello-service-tls, or remove the tls block of the Ingress if your ingress controller terminates TLS for you. Put its address in the inventory as helloUrl: it is printed on the handouts. The service's README lists what it answers.

docs.title: 3 · What browsers must reach
docs.text:
From the participant's browser For The Test Suite and its identity provider The IDE The hello service Chapter 3, from the IDE and from TestLab on the laptop api.openai.com, api.anthropic.com, the Catena-X AI endpoint The assistant. The call goes from the browser, not from the Test Suite. localhost, for a model on the participant's own laptop The assistant, local option github.com Fork, push, pull request

A venue network that blocks one of the model providers blocks the assistant for everyone who uses it. Test it on the guest network, not on yours.

docs.title: 4 · Smoke test
docs.text:
Do the tutorial's chapters 3 to 6 once, from a guest laptop, with the template unchanged:

  1. Sign in, open the IDE, do chapter 3 against the hello service: green.
  2. Connect a model, get an answer.
  3. Open the template, press Compile: it must pass.
  4. Press Run with the values of one team's handout: both tests must pass.

The template's first test needs something behind the provider's connector to call. The workflow uses a small echo service for that; deploy one per pair, or point product_internal_url at any HTTP service the provider's data plane can reach.

docs.title: The session
docs.text:
The table assumes about 75 minutes of work. A dry run with a first-time reader came to about 90, most of the difference in chapters 5 and 6. With a longer slot, give the extra time to chapters 5 and 6, and keep the two checkpoints.

Minute Teams are in Host says Floor looks for 0 1 · Start here "Read box A. Pick Driver, Navigator, Skeptic." Teams with an empty box on the handout 5 2 · Your product "Read your scenario. Press Fork now." Teams that cannot find a refusal: suggest "what was never offered is not found" 10 3 · Hello, TestLab "Write the first test yourself. No AI yet." Teams stuck on indentation: point them to the finished files in the chapter 25 4 · Choose your AI "Hands up when your assistant has answered." Teams without a model: seat them with a team that has one 30 5 · Build "Plan first. Do not let it write before you agree with the plan." Teams whose compile stays red after three rounds 45 6 · Run Checkpoint: "Who has a green compile?" Git push problems, missing sign-off 65 8 · Pull request "Open it as a draft. Then come and ring the bell." ECA check red: the commit email is wrong 70 9 · Next "Two teams: what did the assistant get wrong?" Collect the answers 75 Done "Count the pull requests on the wall."

docs.title: Keep it fun
docs.text:
• The wall. Show the list of pull requests on the room screen. Every new one gets applause. A search for is:pr "E2E test" org:eclipse-tractusx created:>=2026-12-03 is enough.
  • The bell. A real one. A team rings it when its pull request is open.
  • The Skeptic's prize. At minute 55, ask for the best mistake a Skeptic caught. That story is worth more than the fastest team.

docs.title: When a team falls behind
docs.text: Behind at Do Minute 25, no API key but an AI coding assistant on the laptop Send them down the route C. It needs Python and a git clone, so decide early. Minute 35, no assistant Give them the worked example to read and adapt by hand, or seat them with another team. Minute 50, compile still red Have them open the template again and change only the names. A small green test beats a large red one. Minute 60, no green run Skip the run. Go to chapter 7: the workflow will run the test in CI. Minute 70, no push A pull request to their own fork still counts on the wall.

docs.text:
• Note which products now have a pull request. Update the count in your report.
  • Collect what the assistants got wrong. It is input for the starter prompts.
  • Tell the committers of each product that a pull request is waiting, and that a first-time contributor's workflow needs their approval to run.
  • Reset or delete the workshop accounts and connectors, as described in Configure.

docs.title: Choose your AI option
docs.text:
There are three ways to get AI help for your test. Pick the one that fits your laptop and what you already have. All of them end the same way: a TCK project that compiles in the IDE.

Home

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Option You need Speed Quality Best for A · API key in the IDE A key from OpenAI, Anthropic or Catena-X AI Seconds Best Most people B · Local model in the IDE A model server on your laptop (Ollama, LM Studio) Depends on your laptop Good for small, clear changes No key, or nothing may leave your machine C · Your own AI tool, then upload Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor or Codex on your laptop Seconds Best People who already work with such a tool

docs.title: A · An API key in the IDE
docs.text:
1. Open the IDE and press Ask AI.

  2. Pick the provider and paste your key.

  3. A subscription (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot) is not an API key. With only a subscription, use option C.

  4. The key stays in your browser. What you type goes to the provider you picked.

docs.title: B · A local model in the IDE
docs.text: The model runs on your own laptop. Nothing leaves your machine, and nothing costs money. In the IDE, pick Local / self-hosted LLM and keep Small model mode on.

docs.title: What Small model mode does
docs.text:
A local model is slow to read long instructions and gets lost in them. Small model mode gives it a short version and lets it look things up when it needs them:

Normal mode Small model mode Instructions sent before your question about 29,000 tokens about 3,000 tokens First answer, 3B model, our test laptop 7 minutes 17 seconds How it changes a file Rewrites the whole file Uses one IDE action per change, such as add step, add check or set value. The IDE writes the YAML and compiles. How it answers a question Reads the files you have open The IDE reads the project first and gives the model the overview

docs.title: Which size fits your laptop?
docs.text:
Model size Example Download Memory it needs Laptop What to expect 3B qwen2.5:3b 2 GB about 3 GB 8 GB RAM or more Answers questions. Makes one clear change per message: rename, add or remove a step or a check, add a variable. 7B qwen2.5:7b 5 GB about 6 GB 16 GB RAM The same changes, and longer explanations. 14B qwen2.5:14b 9 GB about 11 GB 32 GB RAM, or a GPU with 12 GB Not tested by us. 30B and more qwen3:30b 18 GB or more 20 GB or more 32–64 GB RAM on Apple Silicon, or a GPU with 24 GB Not tested by us. Closer to option A, if your machine can run it.

Rules of thumb:

  • Apple Silicon (M1 to M4) or a gaming GPU: answers in seconds.
  • A laptop without a GPU: expect a minute or more per step. Prefer option A or C.
  • Pick a model that supports tool calls. Without them the assistant can answer but cannot change files.

docs.title: What we aim for, and the limits
docs.text:
We aim for this: with a 3B model on an ordinary laptop, you can ask, plan, and make the small changes the tutorial needs. In our last trial, on an Apple M3 laptop, qwen2.5:3b and qwen2.5:7b each did all nine of these, in 5 to 20 seconds each:

  • rename the test, and rename a step
  • add a check, add a step, remove a step, and copy a step
  • add a variable
  • answer "Which tests and steps does this project have?" and "Which values can a new step use?"

That was one run per model. Earlier runs, before the IDE took over more of the work, got about one change in ten wrong. Every change is checked and can be undone, so a wrong one costs you a click.

The limits:

  • Small models make small changes. Ask for one change at a time. "Write the whole test" is too much for them: start from the template instead.
  • Each question stands alone. In Small model mode the assistant does not see earlier questions. Name the file in every question, for example In tests/my_test.yaml ….
  • Always read what it changed. Every change is listed above the message box, with Review and Undo.
  • If it keeps failing, switch to option A or C. That is not your fault: it is the size of the model.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
1. Install Ollama.

  2. Download a model and start the server so that the IDE may call it. Replace the address with the address of the IDE:

    ollama pull qwen2.5:3b

    OLLAMA_ORIGINS="https://ide.example.org" OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=8192 ollama serve

  3. In the IDE: Ask AI › Local / self-hosted LLM › Connect. Pick your model.

Note

Small model mode is new. If the IDE you use does not show the Small model mode switch yet, a local model needs 64,000 tokens of context and a fast machine, and the first answer takes minutes. Then take option A or C.

docs.title: C · Your own AI tool, then upload to the IDE
docs.text:
You build the test on your laptop with the AI tool you already use, then open it in the IDE to compile, run and inspect it.

  1. Set up the agent kit for your tool: Set up your AI tool.
  2. Ask your tool for the test, in your product's repository.

  3. Check it on your laptop:

    testlab validate tck/e2e

  4. In the IDE: open the folder or upload the ZIP of tck/e2e, then press Compile and Run.

The full route is chapter 4C · Your own AI tool.

docs.title: No AI at all?
docs.text:
Sit with a team that has one, or change the template by hand. The template already passes; renaming it to your product is a good first test.

docs.title: Set up your AI tool
docs.text:
How to give your own AI coding assistant the agent kit, so that it can write a TCK project. You need this only for the route C, when you build on your laptop instead of with the assistant in the IDE.

Home · Files: agent-kit

docs.title: What the kit is
docs.text:
Part What it does A skill, tractusx-e2e-test Instructions your assistant loads when you ask for an E2E test: the way of working, the syntax, the patterns, the template, the worked example and a review checklist An agent, e2e-test-author A ready-made test author that uses the skill. Claude Code only. AGENTS.md The same instructions in five lines, for tools without skills

The skill follows the open Agent Skills format: a folder with a SKILL.md. Several assistants read it. They differ only in where they look for it.

docs.title: First, for every tool
docs.text:
pip install "tractusx-testlab==1.0.0a24"
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/eclipse-tractusx/tutorial-resources.git
cd tutorial-resources/e2e-testing/agent-kit

Then pick your tool.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
Terminal, the VS Code extension and the desktop app share one setup. A Claude subscription is enough: no API key.

  1. Install the skill and the agent:

    ./install.sh claude

    It copies the skill to ~/.claude/skills/tractusx-e2e-test and the agent to ~/.claude/agents/e2e-test-author.md.

  2. Open your product's repository in Claude Code and start a new session.

  3. Type / and check that tractusx-e2e-test is in the list.
  4. Ask for your test. Start with Use the tractusx-e2e-test skill. or, to hand the whole job to the agent, with Use the e2e-test-author agent.

docs.title: GitHub Copilot in VS Code
docs.text:
1. Install the skill:

    ./install.sh copilot

    It copies the skill to ~/.copilot/skills/tractusx-e2e-test.

  2. Open your product's repository in VS Code and open the Chat view.

  3. Choose the mode in which Copilot may edit files and run terminal commands.
  4. Type / and check that tractusx-e2e-test is in the list. Then ask for your test.
  5. Allow Copilot to run testlab validate when it asks.

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
1. Install the skill:

    ./install.sh cursor

    It copies the skill to ~/.cursor/skills/tractusx-e2e-test. Cursor also reads ~/.claude/skills, so ./install.sh claude works too.

  2. Open your product's repository in Cursor and start a new Agent chat.

  3. Type / and check that tractusx-e2e-test is in the list. Then ask for your test.

docs.title: OpenAI Codex
docs.text:
1. Install the skill:

    ./install.sh codex

    It copies the skill to ~/.agents/skills/tractusx-e2e-test.

  2. Start Codex in your product's repository.

  3. Type /skills and check that tractusx-e2e-test is listed. Then ask for your test; $tractusx-e2e-test names the skill in a message.

docs.title: Any other assistant that can read files
docs.text:
No installation. Start your first message with the path to the kit:

Read ../tutorial-resources/e2e-testing/agent-kit/AGENTS.md and follow it.

If your tool only reads files inside the open folder, copy the kit into your repository first and keep it out of Git:

cp -R ../tutorial-resources/e2e-testing/agent-kit .agent-kit
echo ".agent-kit/" >> .git/info/exclude

Then write Read .agent-kit/AGENTS.md and follow it.

docs.title: A chat app without file access
docs.text:
ChatGPT, Claude or another chat in the browser. It works, with you as the hands.

  1. Upload these files from agent-kit/skills/tractusx-e2e-test to the chat: SKILL.md, the three files in reference/, and the three YAML files in assets/template/.

  2. Generate the step catalog and upload it too:

    testlab docs -o - > tck-steps.md

  3. Send the prompt from the route C, step 5.

  4. Save each file the chat gives you under tck/e2e in your repository.
  5. Run testlab validate tck/e2e/index.yaml and paste the output back. Repeat until it prints OK.

docs.title: How to tell it worked
docs.text:
Ask your assistant, before anything else:

Which steps does a TCK test have for reading a twin from a Digital Twin Registry through a connector?

A good answer names real steps such as digital-twin-registry/consumer/dataplane/get_shell_descriptor, and says it looked them up with testlab docs. An answer with invented names means the skill was not loaded: start a new chat, or use the AGENTS.md line above.

docs.text:

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Every term the tutorial links to, in one or two lines. Simple, but not wrong.

Home

docs.title: The test
docs.text: Term What it means E2E test End-to-end test. It uses a product the way a partner would, through the same doors, and checks that the promise holds. It does not look inside the product. TCK Test Compatibility Kit. A package of tests that proves a system does what a standard or an API promises. In this tutorial the E2E test of a product is a TCK. TCK project The editable form of a TCK: a folder with index.yaml, a tests/ folder and optional schemas/ and testdata/. This is what you commit. Manifest The file index.yaml. It names the TCK, lists its tests, declares its variables and says what a run needs on each side. Step One action in a test, such as "create an asset" or "negotiate a contract". A step takes values in (with), gives values back (returns) and checks them (validate). Setup, execution, teardown The three phases of a test: prepare what is needed, do the thing and check it, remove what was created. Positive, negative and contract test Does the promise hold? Is the wrong thing refused? Does the answer have the agreed shape? Validate, compile, run Validate checks the files. Compile packs the project into one .tck package. Run executes the package against real systems and reports PASS or FAIL. SUT System under test. Your product, and the connector in front of it. Engine The side that runs the test. It acts as the partner company and has a connector of its own. TestLab The open-source test engine of Eclipse Tractus-X (tractusx-testlab). It validates, compiles and runs TCKs, from the command line or behind the IDE. Test Suite IDE A browser tool for building TCK projects with blocks, a YAML editor and an AI assistant. Provided by the Catena-X Association. It produces plain TCK projects.

docs.title: The dataspace
docs.text: Term What it means Dataspace A set of rules and building blocks that lets companies exchange data directly, each keeping control of its own data. There is no central database. Participant A company in the dataspace. It has an identity, a wallet and at least one connector. BPN Business Partner Number. The number that identifies a company, for example BPNL000000000001. The L stands for legal entity. DID Decentralized Identifier. The digital identity of a participant, for example did:web:provider.example:BPNL000000000001. Current connectors identify each other by DID; the BPN is still what people and applications use. BDRS BPN-DID Resolution Service. The directory that translates a BPN into a DID. Connector The component through which a participant offers and consumes data. Every exchange between two companies goes from connector to connector. The Tractus-X connector is built on the Eclipse Dataspace Components (EDC). Control plane and data plane The two halves of a connector. The control plane handles catalogs, contracts and transfers. The data plane carries the actual data once a contract exists. Management API The interface a company uses to operate its own connector: create assets and policies, start negotiations. It is protected by an API key and never exposed to partners. DSP Dataspace Protocol. The language two connectors speak to each other: catalog, negotiation, transfer. The DSP address is where a partner reaches your connector. Asset and offer An asset is something a provider makes available, for example an API. An offer is the asset plus the policy under which a partner may use it. A catalog is a list of offers. Policy The terms of an offer, written so that a machine can check them: who may see it (access policy) and what it may be used for (usage policy). Contract agreement The result of a successful negotiation: both connectors have agreed on an offer. EDR Endpoint Data Reference. A short-lived token and an address the consumer receives after a contract is agreed. With it the consumer fetches the data from the provider's data plane. Wallet Holds a participant's verifiable credentials and presents them on request. In Tractus-X this is the IdentityHub. Verifiable credential A digitally signed proof, for example "this company is a member of the dataspace". Connectors check them during a negotiation. Digital twin The digital description of a real thing, such as a part or a vehicle. It says which data exists about the thing and where to get it. Digital Twin Registry The service in which a provider lists its digital twins so that partners can find them. Also called DTR. An entry is a shell descriptor; the pointers to the actual data are submodel descriptors. Eclipse Tractus-X developer toolbox The small dataspace the E2E workflow creates in memory inside the GitHub runner: two connectors, two wallets, a Digital Twin Registry, a BDRS and an IssuerService in a Kubernetes cluster in Docker. It is built from the Umbrella chart with a fixed dataspace configuration, and it is thrown away when the job ends. It is part of the Tractus-X Starter Kit. More. Umbrella The Tractus-X Umbrella is a Helm chart that deploys the Tractus-X products together as one small dataspace. The developer toolbox is built from it.

docs.title: The repository
docs.text:
Term What it means .tractusx metafile A YAML file in the root of every Tractus-X repository. It names the product and its repositories, so that tools can check them. This tutorial adds the link to the E2E test. Leading repository The main repository of a product that is spread over several repositories. The E2E test lives there. TRG Tractus-X Release Guideline. A numbered rule every product follows, for example "every repository has a .tractusx metafile" (TRG 2.05). ECA Eclipse Contributor Agreement. You sign it once with your Eclipse account. A pull request to an Eclipse project is only accepted when the email of its commits belongs to an account with a signed ECA. Signed-off commit A commit whose message ends with Signed-off-by: Your Name <your@email>. git commit -s adds the line. Reusable workflow A GitHub Actions workflow kept in one place and called from other repositories in a few lines. The E2E test workflow is one. Fork and pull request A fork is your own copy of a repository on GitHub. A pull request asks the original repository to take a change from your fork.

docs.title: The .tractusx link
docs.text:
Every Tractus-X repository has a .tractusx metafile in its root. Add one block so that people and tools can find your E2E test.

Home

docs.title: Add this block
docs.text:
e2eTests:
  - name: "Digital Twin Registry E2E test"
    path: "tck/e2e"
    workflow: ".github/workflows/e2e-test.yml"
Field Meaning name What the test is called, for a human. path The folder that holds index.yaml, from the root of the repository. workflow The workflow that runs it.

A complete file is in the worked example.

docs.title: Where it goes
docs.text:
In the leading repository of your product, next to the fields that are already there:

product: "Digital Twin Registry"
leadingRepository: "https://github.com/eclipse-tractusx/sldt-digital-twin-registry"
repositories:
  - name: "sldt-digital-twin-registry"
    usage: "This is the repository which contains the source code for the SLDT digital twin registry"
    url: "https://github.com/eclipse-tractusx/sldt-digital-twin-registry.git"

e2eTests:
  - name: "Digital Twin Registry E2E test"
    path: "tck/e2e"
    workflow: ".github/workflows/e2e-test.yml"

Important

e2eTests is a proposed field. It is defined in the draft TRG for E2E tests, and the name is an open decision there. Metafiles already carry fields the release checks do not read, such as openApiSpecs, so an extra field does not break them.

docs.title: 2 · A GitHub account that may contribute to Eclipse
docs.text:
Your pull request goes to an Eclipse project. Two things must be true:

  • You have an Eclipse account and have signed the Eclipse Contributor Agreement (ECA).
  • The email of your Git commits is the email of that Eclipse account.

Check the second one:

git config user.email

A different email is the usual reason the ECA check on a pull request turns red.

docs.title: 3 · Git that can push
docs.text:
git --version

Make sure a git push to one of your own GitHub repositories works from this laptop, with a token or an SSH key. If you have never pushed from it, do it once now.

docs.title: 4 · A model for the assistant
docs.text:
You bring your own. No key is shared in the workshop. One of these is enough. Not sure which? See Choose your AI option.

Option What you need Good to know OpenAI An API key from the OpenAI developer platform A ChatGPT subscription is not an API key. Anthropic An API key from the Anthropic console A Claude subscription is not an API key. Catena-X AI Your Catena-X AI key and agent ID For members who have access. Local or self-hosted A server with an OpenAI-compatible API, for example Ollama or LM Studio, and a model that supports tool calls Nothing leaves your machine. The server must allow the IDE's address as an origin. With Small model mode, qwen2.5:3b runs on a laptop with 8 GB of RAM: see AI options. Download it at home first.

The key stays in your browser.

Only a subscription, such as Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot, and no API key? Then build with your own assistant on your laptop: install it beforehand, and see Set up your AI tool. This route also needs step 5 below.

No model at all? Sit with a team that has one. You can also write the YAML by hand: the template and the worked example show how.

docs.title: 5 · Optional: the command line
docs.text:
You do not need it in the workshop. The IDE compiles and runs for you, and GitHub Actions does the same in CI. If you like a terminal, with Python 3.12 or newer:

pip install "tractusx-testlab==1.0.0a24"
testlab --help

You should see the commands validate, compile, inspect and run.

docs.text:
• Browser is current.
  • ECA is signed, and git config user.email shows the same email.
  • git push works from this laptop.
  • You have a key or a local model for the assistant.

docs.title: Starter prompts
docs.text:
Paste them into Ask AI in the IDE. Replace the parts in <angle brackets>. Each prompt says which mode to use: Ask, Plan or Agent.

Home · Where the AI helps

docs.title: 1 · Plan the test
docs.text:
Mode: Plan. Use it in chapter 5.

I am building the first E2E test for the Eclipse Tractus-X product
"<product name>" (<repository URL>).

What it must prove (the scenario from the handout):
"<the scenario>"

The open project is a template. Plan how to turn it into this test:
- Keep the two-sided shape: my product is behind the "sut" connector, the
  test runs from the "engine" connector as a partner would.
- One positive test for what a partner can do, one negative test for
  what is refused.
- Use only steps from the block catalog. Do not invent step names.
- Every check must be able to fail: say for each one what the product would
  have to do wrong for it to turn red.
- Addresses, BPNs and keys never go into a test file. Use variables or
  infrastructure references.
- Everything a test creates is removed again in teardown.
- Rename every "my-product" and "My Product" in the template to
  "<product-id>" and "<product name>".

Do not write files yet. Ask me what you do not know.

docs.title: 2 · Fix what the compiler reports
docs.text:
Mode: Agent.

Compile the project and fix what the compiler reports. Change nothing else.

docs.title: 3 · Add a refusal
docs.text:
Mode: Agent.

Add one more negative test: <what must be refused, and how the product
says so, e.g. "a request without a token is answered with 401 or 403">.
Use only steps from the block catalog. Register the test in index.yaml.
Then compile and fix what the compiler reports.

docs.title: 4 · Check the shape of an answer
docs.text:
Mode: Agent. Have the JSON schema ready, or the link to it.

Add a JSON schema check to the step "<step name>": the answer must match
this schema. Put the schema in the project's schemas folder, register it in
index.yaml and reference it from the step.

<paste the schema, or its URL>

docs.title: 5 · Let it play the Skeptic
docs.text:
Mode: Ask.

Review the open project like a maintainer who has to trust a red result.
For every check: can it fail, and what would a failure tell me?
List the checks that can never fail, and the things the tests assume but
do not check. Do not change anything.

docs.title: 6 · Start from an OpenAPI document
docs.text:
Mode: none, this is a menu. For a product whose API a partner calls directly.

  1. Choose File, then Import OpenAPI….
  2. Under Spec source, choose URL and paste the link to your product's OpenAPI document. The catalog tells you whether your product publishes one.
  3. Under Test cases, keep Success response and add at least one refusal, for example Unknown id → 404.
  4. Press Translate. Nothing changes in your project until you apply the result.

Then check the result with prompt 5.

docs.title: 7 · Write the pull request text
docs.text:
Mode: Ask.

Write the description for a pull request that adds this E2E test to
<repository>. Three short parts: what the test proves (one sentence per
test), what a run needs, and how it runs in CI (the workflow
.github/workflows/e2e-test.yml). Plain Markdown, no headings above level 2.

docs.title: When the assistant goes wrong
docs.text:
It does this Say this Invents a step That step does not exist. Use only steps from the block catalog. Writes an address into a test No addresses in test files. Use an infrastructure reference or a variable. Checks only "not null" That check cannot fail. Check the value the product promises. Rewrites files you did not ask for Press Undo all, switch to Plan, and ask again in smaller steps.

Note

How the prompts were checked is stated in the pull request that added this page. A model may answer differently on your day: the plan is yours to judge.

docs.title: Syntax cheat sheet
docs.text:
The parts of a TCK project on one page. Full reference: TestLab TCK syntax.

Home · 3 · Hello, TestLab

docs.title: The folder
docs.text:
tck/e2e/
├── index.yaml      the manifest
├── tests/          one file per test
└── schemas/        optional JSON schemas

docs.title: The manifest, index.yaml
docs.text:
kind: tck
syntax: v1-alpha
id: my-product-e2e              # every test repeats this as `namespace`
metadata:
  name: "My Product — E2E test"
  version: "v0.1.0"
env:
  variables:
    - ...
tests:                          # a test not listed here does not run
  - id: says_hello.yaml
    name: The service says hello

docs.title: A test
docs.text:
kind: test
syntax: v1-alpha
namespace: my-product-e2e       # = the manifest's id
id: says-hello
metadata:
  name: "The service says hello"
  version: "v0.1.0"
setup: []                       # optional
execution:                      # the steps
  - id: say_hello
    uses: http/http_request     # the action
    with:                       # its inputs
      url: "${{ env.service_url }}/hello"
    returns:                    # the outputs you use
      status_code: { type: integer }
    validate:                   # the checks
      - uses: validate/assert
        with: { input: status_code, operator: equals, value: 200 }
teardown: []                    # optional, runs even after a failure

See an action's inputs and outputs with testlab docs -s http/http_request -o -, or in the IDE's toolbox.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Write To get ${{ env.<id> }} A variable from the manifest ${{ execution.<step>.<output> }} An output of an earlier step (setup. for setup steps) ${{ infrastructure.sut.connector.dsp_url }} The connector under test

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
- id: service_url
  uses: variable/type/string
  with:
    source: value               # or `input` with `scope: sut`, to ask at run time
    value: "http://localhost:8080"
  returns:
    value: { type: string }

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
uses Checks validate/assert One output: input, operator, value validate/field A field inside an output: adds path validate/schema An output against a JSON schema

Common operators: equals, contains, not_empty, gt, lt, matches_regex.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
testlab validate index.yaml
testlab compile index.yaml -o my.tck
testlab run index.yaml --yes

docs.title: The developer toolbox
docs.text:
An E2E test needs a small dataspace: two companies, each with a connector and a wallet. The Eclipse Tractus-X developer toolbox is that dataspace. It is part of the Eclipse Tractus-X Starter Kit. The workflow builds it inside the GitHub runner for every run and deletes it afterwards.

Home · The workflow

docs.title: What is in it
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    TL["TestLab"] --> CC
    subgraph kind["kind cluster in the GitHub runner"]
        CC["Partner connector<br/>(engine)"] <-- "catalog, contract, data" --> PC["Your connector<br/>(SUT)"]
        PC --> P["Your product<br/>or the echo service"]
        ISS["Issuer + BDRS"] -. "credentials" .-> CC
        ISS -. "credentials" .-> PC
    end
  • Two connectors with wallets: yours (the SUT) and a partner's (the engine).
  • Trust services: the IssuerService hands out the Catena-X credentials; BDRS maps a BPN to a DID.
  • Digital Twin Registry and an echo service that stands in for your product.

It is the Tractus-X Umbrella chart 26.03.00 on a kind cluster. Every version is pinned.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
The toolbox is the developer-toolbox action in the Tractus-X Starter Kit: the bring-up steps, the Helm values and the helper scripts. You can use it in any workflow, not only this one:

- uses: eclipse-tractusx/tractusx-starter-kit/developer-toolbox@main
  id: toolbox
- run: testlab run my.tck --config "${{ steps.toolbox.outputs.variables-file }}"

docs.title: How a run works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Your repo<br/>12-line workflow"] --> B["1 · Validate and compile<br/>~30 s"] --> C["2 · Toolbox: deploy,<br/>credentials, preflight, run<br/>~6 min"] --> D["Check on the PR"]
  1. Validate and compile your project into a .tck package.
  2. Build the toolbox, issue credentials, check every service answers.
  3. Run the package and report the result on the pull request.

Your repository holds only the test and 12 lines of workflow. The workflow lives in this repository and the toolbox in the Starter Kit, so one change there updates every product.

If a run fails, download the artifacts: e2e-test-run-… has every request and answer, toolbox-diagnostics-… the logs of every pod.

docs.title: Your test never names a host
docs.text: It asks for a side and a capability, for example ${{ infrastructure.sut.connector.dsp_url }}. The workflow fills in the addresses (list). So the same test runs in the toolbox, at the workshop and in your own environment.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• It runs released images. To test your pull request's code, see the workflow.
  • Only products in the Umbrella chart run there. Others set run-in-toolbox: false.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Find the symptom, try the fix, raise your hand if it does not help.

Home

docs.title: The assistant
docs.text: Symptom Try It says the key is not valid Copy the key again, without spaces. A ChatGPT or Claude subscription is not an API key. A local model cannot be reached The server must allow the IDE's address as an origin (CORS), and the address must end in /v1. A local model answers as if it never heard of TCKs Switch on Small model mode in the assistant's settings. Without it, the IDE sends about 29,000 tokens before your first question, and the model needs 64,000 tokens of context. A local model "thinks" for minutes and never answers Switch on Small model mode: the first answer then takes about 20 seconds instead of 7 minutes. On a laptop without a GPU it can still take a minute or more. Then use a hosted model, or the own AI tool route. A local model changes the wrong thing Ask for one change per message, and name the file and the step, for example In tests/my_test.yaml add a check to the step find_offer: datasets is not null. Undo the wrong change above the message box. It invents steps Say: Use only steps from the block catalog. Smaller models need the reminder. It stops halfway Say: Continue. Or ask for one test at a time. It changed files you did not want changed Press Undo all, switch to Plan, ask again in smaller steps.

docs.title: Compile
docs.text: Symptom Try Compile stays red after three rounds Switch to Ask, paste the finding, and ask what the compiler expects there before letting the assistant edit again. "unknown step" The uses: name does not exist. Ask the assistant which step from the catalog does that job. A reference cannot be resolved A ${{ ... }} points at a step or variable that is not there. Check the spelling of the step id. Everything is red and you are out of time Open the template again and change only the names. A small green test beats a large red one.

docs.title: Run
docs.text: Symptom Try The run fails at once: "requires infrastructure that is not fully bound: engine.connector" The connector the tests run from is not set up for your organization. That is the administrators' part: go to the Desk. The run waits and nothing happens Give it a minute. Then ask at the Desk whether your connectors are up. The first step fails with a connection error A value from the handout is mistyped. Compare box C and box D character by character. The negotiation is refused The usage policy of your test asks for something the partner cannot prove. Use the policies of the template unchanged first. The data plane answers 502 The address "as the connector reaches it" is wrong or not reachable from the connector. A step is red and you cannot tell why Open the step and read the request and the answer. Decide: is it the environment, or is it a finding?

docs.title: Git and GitHub
docs.text: Symptom Try git push asks for a password and refuses it GitHub needs a token or an SSH key, not your password. A teammate whose laptop can push can be the Driver. The ECA check on the pull request is red The email of your commit is not the one of your Eclipse account. Fix it with git config user.email, then git commit --amend -s --reset-author and git push --force-with-lease. The checks say "waiting for approval" Normal for a first contribution to a repository. A committer of the product has to approve the run. You want to see the workflow run without waiting Open a second pull request inside your fork, from your branch to your fork's main. It runs at once. The workflow cannot find e2e-test.yml@main The reusable workflow is not published yet. Ask a facilitator for the reference to use.

docs.title: The workflow is red
docs.text: Where Meaning Validate and compile The project in the repository is not the one that compiled in the IDE. Did all files arrive? Check tck/e2e/index.yaml and tck/e2e/tests/. A deploy step of Run in Eclipse Tractus-X developer toolbox The environment, not your test. Run the job again. testlab run A finding, or a value your test expects that the developer toolbox does not provide. Read E2E test result on the run page. PreviousThe .tractusx linkHome

docs.title: The worked example
docs.text:
A complete E2E test project for the Digital Twin Registry (sldt-digital-twin-registry). It validates, compiles and passes in GitHub Actions, in about five and a half minutes.

Home · Files: examples/digital-twin-registry

docs.title: What it proves
docs.text: A partner finds and reads a twin through the owner's connector, and a twin that does not exist is refused with "not found".

docs.title: What is in the folder
docs.text:
examples/digital-twin-registry/
├── .tractusx                               the metafile, with the link to the test
├── .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml          the workflow: 12 lines that matter
└── tck/e2e/
    ├── index.yaml                          the manifest
    ├── schemas/shell_descriptor.json       the shape a twin must have
    └── tests/
        ├── register_and_read.yaml          positive + contract
        ├── partner_reads_through_connector.yaml   the journey
        └── unknown_twin_is_not_found.yaml  negative

docs.title: The three tests
docs.text: Test Kind What happens Register and read Positive, contract The owner registers a twin, reads it back, and both answers are checked against the JSON schema. The twin is removed. A partner reads through the connector Positive, the journey Setup offers the registry in the owner's connector and registers a twin the partner may see. The test negotiates access, finds the twin by its part number and reads it. Everything is removed. An unknown twin is not found Negative The registry is asked for a twin it never held and must answer 404.

docs.title: What a run prints
docs.text:
TCK RUN SUMMARY
  ✓ Register and read                          PASS
  ✓ A partner reads through the connector      PASS
  ✓ An unknown twin is not found               PASS
RESULT: PASS  |  3 passed  0 failed  0 skipped

docs.title: It failed first, and that was useful
docs.text:
The first run in CI was red:

✗ partner-reads-through-connector[read_twin]  FAIL
  Schema validation failed (1 error(s)): submodelDescriptors: [] should be non-empty

The test had registered a twin without any pointer to data. The schema check caught it: a twin with no submodel descriptor is of no use to a partner. The fix was one more setup step, create_submodel.

That is what a contract check is for. A check on "status 200" would have stayed green.

docs.title: Read it in this order
docs.text:
1. index.yaml: look at infrastructure, then at tests.
  2. unknown_twin_is_not_found.yaml: the smallest possible test, one step and one check.
  3. partner_reads_through_connector.yaml: setup, execution, teardown.

docs.title: Run it yourself
docs.text:
With Python 3.12 or newer:

pip install "tractusx-testlab==1.0.0a24"
cd e2e-testing/examples/digital-twin-registry/tck/e2e
testlab validate index.yaml
testlab compile index.yaml -o /tmp/dtr-e2e.tck
testlab inspect /tmp/dtr-e2e.tck --variables --infrastructure

validate ends with OK — index.yaml is valid (no issues). inspect lists 3 tests, 19 steps and 13 checks.

To run it you need two connectors and a registry. The workflow creates them for you.

docs.title: The workflow
docs.text:
A test that somebody has to remember to run will not be run. This workflow runs it on every pull request.

Home

docs.title: Copy these lines
docs.text:
Save as .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml in your repository. The full file with its licence header is in the worked example.

name: E2E test

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: e2e-test-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  e2e:
    name: E2E test
    uses: eclipse-tractusx/tutorial-resources/.github/workflows/e2e-test.yml@main
    with:
      tck-directory: tck/e2e

That is all a product repository needs. The work happens in the reusable workflow it calls.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    PR["Pull request"] --> V["Validate and compile<br/>about 30 seconds"]
    V --> P[".tck package"]
    P --> E["Run in Eclipse Tractus-X developer toolbox<br/>about 5 minutes"]
    E --> R["PASS or FAIL<br/>on the pull request"]
Job Needs Tells the maintainers Validate and compile Nothing but Python The test project is well-formed and still compiles. Run in Eclipse Tractus-X developer toolbox A dataspace, which the job creates itself The product still keeps its promise.

On the fork where it was proven, the first job took 23 seconds and the second 4 minutes 57 seconds.

The second job starts the Eclipse Tractus-X developer toolbox: a Kubernetes cluster inside the runner with two connectors, two wallets, a Digital Twin Registry, a BDRS and an IssuerService, deployed from the Tractus-X Umbrella chart. It issues the participants' credentials, runs the package and throws everything away. No secrets, no external cluster. The developer toolbox shows what is in it and how it comes up.

The developer toolbox lives in the Tractus-X Starter Kit, as the developer-toolbox action. The workflow calls it in one step and runs your package against the values it returns.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Default Use it to tck-directory tck/e2e Point at the folder that holds index.yaml. testlab-version 1.0.0a24 Pin the TestLab version that validates, compiles and runs. run-in-toolbox true Set to false to only validate and compile, for a product the developer toolbox cannot run yet. config none Add run values of your own: a YAML file with variables:. toolbox-values none Add Helm values to the developer toolbox, for example the image built from this pull request.

docs.title: Values your test gets for free
docs.text:
The workflow fills in everything about the dataspace it created:

Value What it is infrastructure.sut.connector.* The provider's connector: your side infrastructure.engine.connector.* The consumer's connector: the partner side infrastructure.sut.dtr.base_url The provider's Digital Twin Registry sut_bpnl, engine_bpnl The two BPNs dtr_internal_url The registry as the provider's connector reaches it product_internal_url A small echo service behind the provider's connector: a stand-in for a product

Anything else your project declares as an input goes into a file of your own, named with the config input:

variables:
  my_own_value: "something"

docs.title: Test the image from your pull request
docs.text:
Out of the box the developer toolbox deploys released images. To test the code of the pull request, build your image in a job of your own and pass its tag as Helm values:

    with:
      tck-directory: tck/e2e
      toolbox-values: tck/e2e/ci/values.yaml

Note

The toolbox-values input is applied by the workflow, but this page's example of building and loading an image was not run. Loading a locally built image into the cluster needs one more step in your own workflow.

docs.title: How it was checked
docs.text: Check Result actionlint Passes. Four style notes come from the steps taken over from TestLab. Real run on a fork of this repository, worked example 3 tests passed Real run on a fork of this repository, template 2 tests passed Real run in a fork of sldt-digital-twin-registry, called across repositories, with the project exported from the IDE 3 tests passed, 5 minutes 25 seconds in total config and toolbox-values inputs Not run with a file of a calling repository

docs.title: When it is red
docs.text:
1. Open the failed job and read E2E test result on the run page.
  2. A failed check is a finding: the product answered, and not as promised.
  3. A failed deploy step is the environment. Download the toolbox-diagnostics artifact: it holds the state and the logs of every pod.

docs.title: E2E test specs
docs.text:
You don't need to know your product. Its spec says what the test must prove, which steps to use and what the finished TCK looks like. You and your assistant turn it into YAML, make it green and open the pull request.

Home · Product catalog · Glossary

docs.title: Pick your product
docs.text:
Product What the test proves Tests Runs in the workshop Spec Business Partner Data Management (BPDM) A business partner a member uploads to the Gate can be read back, and the Gate refuses a caller without a token. 2 + 1 optional Build and compile only Draft BPN-DID Resolution Service (BDRS) A partner is found and its catalog is reached with nothing but its BPN, and it resolves to the right identity. 3 Yes Draft Digital Twin Registry A partner finds a twin by its part number and reads it through the owner's connector, and a twin that does not exist is not found. 3 + 1 optional Yes Proven Tractus-X EDC (connector) A partner finds an offer in the catalog, negotiates a contract and gets the data, and without a token it gets nothing. 3 + 1 optional Yes Draft Tractus-X IdentityHub (wallet and IssuerService) A partner whose wallet holds the right credentials gets the contract, and an offer meant for another company stays invisible to it. 2 Yes Draft

Proven: a TCK built from the spec passed in GitHub Actions. Draft: not run end to end yet. If something in a draft does not hold, tell a facilitator: your finding fixes the spec.

docs.title: Every spec has the same eight parts
docs.text: Part Tells you 1 · The product What it does, for someone who has never heard of it 2 · The journey The story, move by move, between your side and the partner side 3 · The TCK you deliver Folder, manifest fields, variables, schemas 4 · The tests Each test, phase by phase: step, what happens, what must be true 5 · Break it on purpose How to see each check fail for the right reason 6 · Watch out What went wrong before 7 · Not in this spec What you do not need to test today 8 · Give it to your assistant The prompt, and the raw spec to attach

docs.title: The target TCK, for every product
docs.text:
<product repository>/
├── tck/e2e/
│   ├── index.yaml        # the manifest: id <product>-e2e, kind tck, syntax v1-alpha
│   ├── tests/            # one file per test, each with setup, execution, teardown
│   └── schemas/          # only when a test checks an answer against a JSON schema
├── .tractusx             # e2eTest: tck/e2e

docs.title: 1 · The product in brief
docs.text: A company lists its parts in the registry as "digital twins": one shell descriptor per part, with the part numbers it is known by and a pointer to where its data is. A partner who knows a part number asks the registry, through the owner's connector, which twin belongs to it. Without the registry, a partner cannot find any data.

docs.text:
A partner finds an offer in the catalog, negotiates a contract and gets the data, and without a token it gets nothing.

Repository: tractusx-edc · Spec 1.0 · Draft · Raw spec for your AI · All specs

Note

Tests 1 and 2 follow the template, which passes in GitHub Actions. Tests 3 and 4 have not been run yet: confirm the status code of test 3 in the first run.

docs.title: 1 · The product in brief
docs.text: The connector is the door of a company to the dataspace. A provider puts data behind it as an "asset" and publishes an offer with rules (policies) on who may see it and what it may be used for. A partner's connector asks for the catalog, negotiates a contract and receives a token. With the token it calls the provider's data plane and gets the data.

docs.title: 2 · The journey the test tells
docs.text:
Side Played by Your side (SUT) The provider's connector, with a small echo service behind it as the data Partner side (engine) The partner's connector, where the tests run from
  1. The provider creates an access policy, a usage policy and an asset that points at the echo service.
  2. The provider publishes a contract definition that ties the three together.
  3. The partner asks the provider's catalog for that asset and sees the offer.
  4. The partner negotiates a contract and receives a data plane URL and a token.
  5. The partner calls the data plane with the token and gets the echo service's answer.
  6. The provider removes the offer, the asset and both policies.

A partner whose wallet holds the right credentials gets the contract, and an offer meant for another company stays invisible to it.

Repository: tractusx-identityhub · Spec 1.0 · Draft · Raw spec for your AI · All specs

Note

Not run end to end yet. The test proves the wallet by its effect: the connectors only agree when the partner's credentials are presented and accepted.

docs.title: 1 · The product in brief
docs.text: Every company in the dataspace has a wallet that holds its verifiable credentials: proof that it is a member, which framework agreements it signed, and its BPN. The IssuerService hands these credentials out. When a partner asks for a catalog or a contract, its connector presents the credentials from its wallet, and the provider's connector checks them against the policy.

docs.title: 2 · The journey the test tells
docs.text:
Side Played by Your side (SUT) The provider's connector and wallet Partner side (engine) The partner's connector and wallet, where the tests run from
  1. The provider publishes an offer whose usage policy asks for membership and the DataExchangeGovernance framework agreement.
  2. The partner's connector presents the credentials from its wallet and negotiates.
  3. The provider's connector accepts them, and the contract is agreed.
  4. The provider publishes a second offer that only one other BPN may see.
  5. The partner asks the catalog and does not see the second offer.

docs.text:
The assistant in the IDE knows the catalog of steps and the rules of the format. It does not know what your product promises. That part is yours.

docs.title: Three modes
docs.text:
Mode It does Use it for Ask Answers. Never changes files. "Which steps read a twin through the connector?" Plan Lays out the changes. Never changes files. Seeing whether it understood, before it writes anything Agent Changes your project files. Every change can be undone. Building the test

Start with Plan. A plan costs a few seconds and saves you from forty lines of YAML that test the wrong thing.

docs.title: Three mistakes to look for, every time
docs.text:
Mistake How to spot it An invented step. uses: names something that does not exist. Compile reports it. A check that cannot fail. For example not_null on a value that is always there. Ask: what would the product have to do wrong for this to turn red? An environment written into the test. An address or a BPN inside a test file. Search the YAML for http and BPNL.

None of these is a reason not to use the assistant. They are the reason you read what it wrote.

docs.title: Which model?
docs.text:
You bring your own. The IDE connects from your browser straight to the provider you pick: OpenAI, Anthropic, Catena-X AI, or a server of your own (Ollama, LM Studio or any other server with an OpenAI-compatible API).

  • No key is shared in the workshop, and none is stored on the IDE's server.
  • Larger models follow the step catalog more reliably. A small local model works too: Small model mode gives it short instructions and lets the IDE do the writing. See AI options.
  • What you paste into the assistant goes to the provider you chose. Do not paste secrets.

docs.title: A dataspace in five minutes
docs.text:
Introduction · 2 of 4 · optional reading, 5 minutes

You can follow the tutorial without this page. Read it if words like connector or BPN are new, or if you want to know what your test is actually doing.

docs.title: Two companies, no middleman
docs.text:
A dataspace lets companies exchange data directly, each keeping control of its own. There is no central database. There are rules everyone follows, and a small set of building blocks every participant runs.

Picture two companies. One has data, the other wants it.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Provider["Company A, the provider"]
        P["Product<br/>the data or the service"] --- PC["Connector"]
        PW["Wallet"] -.- PC
    end
    subgraph Consumer["Company B, the consumer"]
        CC["Connector"] -.- CW["Wallet"]
    end
    CC -- "1 What do you offer?" --> PC
    CC -- "2 I accept your terms" --> PC
    CC -- "3 Then give me the data" --> PC

docs.title: The four building blocks you will meet
docs.text:
Block In one line Real-world picture Connector The door of a company to the dataspace. Every exchange goes through it. The goods-in gate with a guard Wallet Holds the company's proofs, for example "I am a member of this dataspace". A folder of stamped certificates Digital Twin Registry A list of the things a company has data about, and where that data is. The index cards of a library BDRS Translates a company number into the company's digital identity. A phone book

Every company has a BPN, a Business Partner Number such as BPNL000000000001. It is how participants name each other.

docs.title: One exchange, three steps
docs.text:
Every data exchange in the dataspace has the same three steps. Your test will walk through them, because your product is reached the same way.

  1. Catalog. The consumer's connector asks the provider's connector: what do you offer me? The answer is a list of offers, each with a policy: the terms of use.
  2. Negotiation. The consumer accepts an offer. Both connectors check each other's proofs from the wallets. If the terms are met, they sign a contract agreement.
  3. Transfer. The consumer receives a short-lived token, the EDR, and uses it to fetch the data through the provider's data plane.

If any proof is missing or the terms are not met, step 2 ends with a refusal. A good test checks the refusal too.

docs.title: Where your product sits
docs.text:
Most Tractus-X products are one of two things:

  • A building block itself, such as the connector, the wallet or the registry.
  • A service behind the connector, such as a traceability application whose API a partner calls through the three steps above.

Either way, the E2E question is the same: can a partner get what your product promises?

docs.title: What the workshop gives you
docs.text:
Every team gets its own small dataspace: two connectors with their wallets, a Digital Twin Registry and a BDRS. One side plays your company with your product. The other side is the partner, and that is where your test runs from.

The same small dataspace is created inside GitHub Actions when your test runs in CI. It is the Eclipse Tractus-X developer toolbox: the Tractus-X Umbrella Helm chart with a small dataspace configuration, in memory in the runner.

docs.title: What a test is made of
docs.text: Introduction · 3 of 4 · optional reading, 5 minutes

docs.title: A TCK is a folder of YAML
docs.text:
TCK stands for Test Compatibility Kit: a package of tests that proves a system does what it promises. A TCK project is the editable form, a folder you commit:

tck/e2e/
├── index.yaml      the manifest: what is tested, what a run needs, which tests belong to it
├── tests/          one file per test
└── schemas/        JSON schemas an answer is checked against (optional)

docs.title: Two sides: the system under test, and the engine
docs.text:
A test always has two parties.

Side Called Who it is today The one being tested SUT, system under test Your product and the connector in front of it The one testing Engine TestLab, acting as the partner through the second connector

The manifest says what each side must bring:

infrastructure:
  engine:
    connector:
      required: true
  sut:
    connector:
      required: true
    dtr:
      required: true

Addresses and keys are not in the project. They are given when the test runs, so the same test runs in the workshop, in CI and in anybody's own environment.

docs.title: A test has three phases
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S["setup<br/>prepare what the test needs"] --> E["execution<br/>do it, and check the answers"] --> T["teardown<br/>remove what was created"]

Each phase is a list of steps. A step uses one ready-made action, passes values in, gets values back, and checks them:

- id: read_twin
  uses: digital-twin-registry/consumer/dataplane/get_shell_descriptor   # the action
  name: Read the twin as the partner                                     # what a human reads
  with:                                                                  # values in
    aas_identifier: "${{ setup.create_shell.id }}"
  validate:                                                              # checks
    - uses: validate/assert
      with: { input: id, operator: equals, value: "${{ setup.create_shell.id }}" }

${{ ... }} refers to a value from somewhere else: an earlier step, a variable, or the infrastructure of the run.

docs.title: Three kinds of check
docs.text:
Kind Question it answers Example Positive Does the promise hold? A partner can read the twin. Negative Is the wrong thing refused? A twin that does not exist is answered with 404. Contract Does the answer have the agreed shape? The twin matches the JSON schema of the standard.

A test that only ever checks "it answered with 200" proves that the system is switched on. An E2E test proves that it keeps a promise.

docs.title: From YAML to a result
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Y["index.yaml + tests"] -- validate --> V["well-formed?"]
    V -- compile --> P[".tck package"]
    P -- run --> R["PASS or FAIL<br/>per test, per step, per check"]
  • Validate checks the files: known steps, known fields, values wired correctly.
  • Compile turns the project into one package, the form that is run and shared.
  • Run executes it against real systems and records every request and answer.

The IDE does all three with buttons. The workflow does all three with the TestLab command line. Same engine, same result.

docs.title: Why we are here
docs.text: Introduction · 1 of 4 · optional reading, 3 minutes

docs.title: A release, three weeks, many people
docs.text:
Eclipse Tractus-X ships its products together, several times a year. Before each release there is an E2E testing phase: typically three weeks, a daily meeting, and one shared integration environment. People deploy every product there and check, case by case, that the products still work together.

It works. It is also the most expensive way to find out that something broke.

What happens today What it costs A change breaks the hand-over between two products Nobody notices until the test phase, weeks later The test phase finds it Someone has to work out which of the changes since the last release did it The fix arrives The whole chain is tested again, by hand

docs.title: Each product tests itself. Nobody tests the journey.
docs.text:
Every product has unit tests. Many have a Helm test that proves the product starts. What is missing is the test a partner would write:

"I am another company. I find your offer, I sign the contract, I ask for the data. Do I get it?"

That is an end-to-end test, an E2E test. It does not care how the product is built. It cares whether the promise holds.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
1. Every product keeps one E2E test in its own repository. The team that knows the product writes it. The test travels with the code.
  2. The test is written in one common format, a TCK: plain YAML made of ready-made steps such as "create an asset" or "negotiate a contract". Nobody has to learn thirty test frameworks to read thirty tests.
  3. The test runs on every pull request, in GitHub Actions, against a small dataspace that is created inside the runner and thrown away afterwards.
  4. The repository says where its test is, in its .tractusx metafile, so tools can find it.

When every product has one, the three weeks before a release get a lot quieter: a broken hand-over shows up as a red check on the pull request that caused it.

docs.title: Why one session is enough
docs.text:
Writing a test like this used to mean days of reading API documents. Three things changed:

  • Ready-made steps. TestLab already knows how to talk to a connector, a Digital Twin Registry and a wallet. You combine steps; you do not program them.
  • An AI assistant that knows the step catalog and writes the YAML while you decide what must be proven.
  • A dataspace in a box. The workflow brings up connectors, wallets and a registry by itself. You do not need a cluster.

docs.title: What we ask of you today
docs.text:
Write the first E2E test for your product. Not the complete one. One journey that matters, one refusal that matters, running in CI and linked from .tractusx.

The second test is much easier than the first. That is the point of today.

docs.text:

You win when your pull request shows a green check.

docs.text:

  2. Read box A: your product, its repository and a suggested scenario.
  3. Open this tutorial on the laptop you will work on. The QR code on the handout leads here.

  5. Give out three roles. Swap them whenever you like.

    Role Does Driver Has the keyboard Navigator Reads the steps aloud, keeps an eye on the clock Skeptic Reads what the assistant writes and asks "can this check ever fail?"

docs.title: 2 · Your product and your connectors
docs.text: Goal: you know your product, your two connectors and the scenario your test will prove. Time: 5 minutes

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open your product's repository (handout, box A) and read in its README what the product does.
  2. Press Fork at the top right of the repository page, then Create fork. Leave the tab open; you need the fork in chapter 7.

  3. Find your product in the product catalog and read its suggested scenario. It is the same as on the handout, box A: what a partner can do with your product, and what is refused. Your test proves both.

    Does your product have an E2E spec? Then read it instead: it says what each test must prove, which steps to use and what the finished TCK looks like. You don't need to work out the product's API yourself. 4. Look at boxes C and D of the handout. They are your two connectors:

    Box Plays In the test it is called C · Your side Your company, with your product SUT, the system under test D · Partner side Another company that uses your product Engine, where the test runs from

docs.title: You should now see
docs.text:
Your fork on GitHub, named <your-user>/<your-product>.

The pilot team's scenario The pilot team got the **Digital Twin Registry**. Their scenario: a partner finds and reads a twin through the owner's connector, and a twin that does not exist is refused with "not found". Their finished project is the [worked example](../reference/worked-example.md).

Tip

Stuck?

  • The scenario has no refusal: "something that was never offered is not found" is always true and always worth checking. The template starts with exactly that.
  • Your product is not behind a connector: then the partner calls its API directly. The scenario stays the same; say so to the assistant in chapter 5.
  • Your product is marked "needs more than the workshop environment" in the catalog: you build and compile today, and skip the run in chapter 6. Tell a facilitator.
